paragraphs.mainIdea: Father Wolf jumps at something in the bushes. He sees a man's cub just in time and stops in the air.
paragraphs.simple: The bushes made a little noise in the thicket. Father Wolf got low, with his back legs under him, ready to jump. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world: the wolf stopped in the middle of his jump. He had jumped before he saw what was there, and then he tried to stop. So he went straight up into the air, four or five feet, and came down almost in the same place where he had left the ground.

paragraphs.simple: Shere Khan had jumped at a woodcutter's campfire, as Father Wolf had said, and he was very angry because his feet hurt from the burns. But Father Wolf knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in. paragraphs.context: The Law of the Jungle lays down very clearly that any wolf may
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Law of the Jungle says that wolf cubs must be shown to the Pack Council. After that, the Pack must not kill them.
paragraphs.simple: The Law of the Jungle says very clearly that a wolf may leave his Pack when he marries. But when his cubs are old enough to stand on their feet, he must bring them to the Pack Council. The Council is usually held once a month, when the moon is full, so that the other wolves can know who the cubs are. After that look, the cubs are free to run where they like. Until they have killed their first buck, no excuse is accepted if a grown wolf of the Pack kills one of them. The punishment is death, if the one who killed them can be found. If you think about it for a minute, you will see that this must be so.

paragraphs.context: A black shadow dropped down into the circle. It was Bagheera
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bagheera the Black Panther comes into the circle. He is feared by everybody, but his voice is very soft.
paragraphs.simple: A black shadow came down into the circle. It was Bagheera, the Black Panther. He was black as ink all over, but in some lights the panther marks showed, like the pattern on watered silk. Everybody knew Bagheera, and nobody wanted to get in his way, because he was as sly as Tabaqui, as brave as the wild buffalo, and as careless of danger as the wounded elephant. But his voice was as soft as wild honey dripping from a tree, and his skin was softer than the softest feathers.

paragraphs.context: By Red Flower Bagheera meant fire, only no creature in the jungle
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bagheera means fire when he says Red Flower. The animals are afraid of fire and never use its real name.
paragraphs.simple: When Bagheera said Red Flower, he meant fire. But no animal in the jungle will call fire by its real name. Every animal is in great fear of it, and finds a hundred ways to talk about it.

paragraphs.context: All this will show you how much Mowgli had to learn by heart
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mowgli is tired of learning. Baloo says that a man's cub must learn all the Law of the Jungle.
paragraphs.simple: All this shows how much Mowgli had to learn by heart. He became very tired of saying the same thing a hundred times. But one day Mowgli had been hit and had run away angry. Then Baloo said to Bagheera, “A man's cub is a man's cub, and he must learn all the Law of the Jungle.”

paragraphs.context: They were always just going to have a leader and laws and customs
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys always say they will have a leader and laws, but they never do. They forget everything by the next day.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys were always just about to have a leader and laws and ways of their own, but they never did. Their memories could not last from one day to the next. So they settled things by making up a saying: “What the Bandar-log think now the Jungle will think later.” That made them feel much better. No animal could reach them, but also no animal would notice them. That was why they were so pleased when Mowgli came to play with them, and when they heard how angry Baloo was.

paragraphs.context: They found him stretched out on a warm ledge in the afternoon sun
paragraphs.mainIdea: Baloo and Bagheera find Kaa the python. He has a new skin and looks very fine.
paragraphs.simple: They found him lying on a warm ledge in the afternoon sun. He was looking with pleasure at his beautiful new coat. For the last ten days he had stayed away from others while he changed his skin, and now he looked very fine. He moved his big head with its blunt nose quickly along the ground. He twisted his thirty feet of body into strange knots and curves, and he licked his lips as he thought of the dinner to come.

paragraphs.context: In the Cold Lairs the Monkey People were not thinking of Mowgli’s friends
paragraphs.mainIdea: The monkeys take Mowgli to an old, broken city. It is very old, and trees and plants grow in the walls.
paragraphs.simple: In the Cold Lairs the Monkey People were not thinking about Mowgli's friends at all. They had brought the boy to the Lost City, and for a while they were very pleased with themselves. Mowgli had never seen a city in India before. It was almost a heap of ruins, but it seemed very wonderful and fine to him. Some king had built it long ago on a little hill. You could still follow the stone roads that went up to the broken gates, where the last bits of wood hung on old, rusty hinges. Trees had grown into and out of the walls. The tops of the walls had fallen down and fallen apart, and wild climbing plants hung from the windows of the towers on the walls in thick bunches.

paragraphs.context: Bagheera gave him half a dozen love-taps
paragraphs.mainIdea: Bagheera punishes Mowgli, but the hits are light for a panther. Mowgli takes it without a word.
paragraphs.simple: Bagheera gave him six soft hits. For a panther they were so light that they would hardly have woken one of his own cubs. But for a seven-year-old boy they were as hard a beating as anyone would want to avoid. When it was over, Mowgli sneezed and got up without a word.

paragraphs.context: the cubs had often nipped Mowgli harder than they intended
paragraphs.mainIdea: The white marks on Mowgli's arms and legs come from the wolf cubs' play. He does not call them bites.
paragraphs.simple: Of course, when the cubs played with Mowgli, they had often bitten him harder than they meant to, and he had white marks all over his arms and legs. But he would never have called these bites, because he knew what real biting was.

paragraphs.context: The priest was a clever man, and he knew that Messua was wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: The priest knows that Messua's husband is rich. So he says that the jungle has given her boy back.
paragraphs.simple: The priest was a clever man, and he knew that Messua was the wife of the richest man in the village. So he looked up at the sky for a minute and said in a serious voice: “What the jungle has taken the jungle has given back. Take the boy into your house, my sister, and do not forget to honor the priest, who can see so far into the lives of men.”

paragraphs.context: For three months after that night Mowgli hardly ever left the village gate
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mowgli learns the ways of men. He is often angry, but he keeps his temper because of the Law of the Jungle.
paragraphs.simple: For three months after that night, Mowgli hardly ever left the village gate, because he was so busy learning the ways of men. First he had to wear a cloth around his body, and this annoyed him very much. Then he had to learn about money, which he did not understand at all, and about plowing, which seemed to him to have no use. Then the little children of the village made him very angry. Luckily, the Law of the Jungle had taught him to keep his temper, because in the jungle life and food depend on it. The children laughed at him because he would not play games or fly kites, or because he said some word wrongly. Only one thing stopped him from picking them up and breaking them in two: he knew that it was not fair to kill little naked cubs.

paragraphs.context: The two wolves ran, ladies’-chain fashion, in and out of the herd
paragraphs.mainIdea: Akela and Gray Brother split the buffalo herd into two groups. The cows and the bulls are in different groups.
paragraphs.simple: The two wolves ran in and out of the herd in a pattern like a dance. The herd snorted, threw up its head, and split into two groups. In one group stood the cow-buffaloes with their calves in the middle. They glared and pawed the ground, ready to charge and trample the life out of a wolf, if one would only stay still. In the other group the bulls and the young bulls snorted and stamped. They looked more grand, but they were much less dangerous, because they had no calves to protect. No six men could have split the herd so well.

paragraphs.context: To do Buldeo justice, if he had been ten years younger he would have
paragraphs.mainIdea: Buldeo sees a wolf obey Mowgli. He thinks it is magic and is afraid.
paragraphs.simple: To be fair to Buldeo, if he had been ten years younger he would have faced Akela if he had met the wolf in the woods. But a wolf that obeyed the orders of this boy, who had private wars with man-eating tigers, was no common animal. Buldeo thought it was sorcery, magic of the worst kind. He wondered if the amulet round his neck would keep him safe. He lay as still as he could, and thought that at any minute he would see Mowgli turn into a tiger too.

paragraphs.context: Ever since Akela had been deposed, the Pack had been without a leader
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Pack has no leader, and many wolves are hurt. They come to the Council Rock and see Shere Khan's hide. Mowgli sings a song.
paragraphs.simple: Since Akela had been taken from his place as leader, the Pack had had no leader, and they hunted and fought as they liked. But they answered the call from habit. Some of them were lame from the traps they had fallen into, some limped from shot wounds, some had bare patches of skin from eating bad food, and many were missing. But all that were left came to the Council Rock. They saw Shere Khan's striped hide on the rock, and the huge claws hanging at the end of the empty feet. Then Mowgli made up a song with no rhymes. It came up into his throat all by itself, and he shouted it out loud. He jumped up and down on the rattling skin and beat time with his heels until he had no breath left, while Gray Brother and Akela howled between the verses.

paragraphs.context: It was not the fashion for Sea Catch to eat anything during
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sea Catch eats nothing for four months, so he is bad-tempered. His wife Matkah knows not to answer back.
paragraphs.simple: Sea Catch did not eat anything during the four months that he stayed on the beaches. That was the custom, and so his temper was usually bad. Matkah knew that she should not answer him back. She looked around and said softly: “How thoughtful of you. You've taken the old place again.”

paragraphs.context: Little seals can no more swim than little children, but they are unhappy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kotick is carried out by a wave on his first time in the sea. He nearly drowns, but the next wave saves him.
paragraphs.simple: Little seals can no more swim than little children can, but they are unhappy until they learn. The first time Kotick went down to the sea, a wave carried him out to where the water was too deep for him. His big head went down and his little back flippers flew up, just as his mother had told him in the song. If the next wave had not thrown him back, he would have drowned.

paragraphs.context: Ten minutes later little Kotick did not recognize his friends any more
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kotick sees the men skin the seals. He is shocked.
paragraphs.simple: Ten minutes later, little Kotick could not know his friends any more. Their skins had been pulled off, from the nose to the back flippers, and thrown on the ground in a pile.

paragraphs.context: That was enough for Kotick. He turned and galloped
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kotick runs back to the sea in fear. A sea-lion talks to him in a rough voice.
paragraphs.simple: That was enough for Kotick. He turned and ran back to the sea (a seal can run very fast for a short time), and his little new mustache stood up straight with fear. At Sea-Lion's Neck, where the big sea-lions sit at the edge of the waves, he threw himself into the cool water with his flippers over his head. He rocked there, breathing hard and feeling very sad. “What's here?” said a sea-lion in a rough voice, because as a rule the sea-lions keep to themselves.

paragraphs.context: They were like no walrus, sea-lion, seal, bear, whale, shark, fish, squid, or scallop
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kotick sees strange big animals in the sea. They look foolish, and they are the sea cows.
paragraphs.simple: They were not like any walrus, sea-lion, seal, bear, whale, shark, fish, squid or scallop that Kotick had seen before. They were between twenty and thirty feet long. They had no back flippers, but a tail like a shovel, that looked as if it had been cut out of wet leather. Their heads were the most foolish-looking things you ever saw. When they were not feeding, they stood on the ends of their tails in deep water, bowing seriously to one another and waving their front flippers the way a fat man waves his arm.

paragraphs.context: Then Kotick dropped his head between his shoulders and shut his eyes proudly
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kotick has won the fight, and he is red with blood. He is too proud to look at his wounds.
paragraphs.simple: Then Kotick put his head down between his shoulders and shut his eyes proudly. He was not a white seal any more, but red from his head to his tail. Still, he would have thought it beneath him to look at or touch one of his wounds.

paragraphs.context: It is the hardest thing in the world to frighten a mongoose
paragraphs.mainIdea: A mongoose is never afraid for long, because he is very curious. Rikki-tikki looks around the room.
paragraphs.simple: It is the hardest thing in the world to frighten a mongoose, because he is full of curiosity from his nose to his tail. The saying of all the mongoose family is “Run and find out,” and Rikki-tikki was a true mongoose. He looked at the cotton-wool and decided that it was not good to eat. He ran all round the table, sat up and made his fur tidy, scratched himself, and jumped on the small boy's shoulder.

paragraphs.context: He spread out his hood more than ever, and Rikki-tikki saw the spectacle-mark
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nag shows his hood, but Rikki-tikki is not afraid for long. A mongoose knows that its work is to fight snakes.
paragraphs.simple: Nag spread out his hood more than ever, and Rikki-tikki saw the spectacle mark on the back of it, which looks exactly like the eye part of a hook-and-eye fastening. For a minute he was afraid. But a mongoose cannot stay frightened for long. Rikki-tikki had never met a live cobra before, but his mother had fed him on dead ones, and he knew that all a grown mongoose has to do in life is fight and eat snakes. Nag knew that too, and deep in his cold heart he was afraid.

paragraphs.context: If you read the old books of natural history, you will find they say
paragraphs.mainIdea: Old books say that a mongoose eats a herb when a snake bites it. The writer says that this is not true: a mongoose wins by being quick.
paragraphs.simple: If you read the old books about nature, you will find that they say a mongoose that is bitten in a fight with a snake runs off and eats a herb that cures him. That is not true. The win is only a matter of a quick eye and a quick foot: the snake's blow against the mongoose's jump. No eye can follow the move of a snake's head when it strikes, and that is much more wonderful than any magic herb. Rikki-tikki knew that he was a young mongoose, and he was even more pleased to think that he had escaped a blow from behind. It gave him trust in himself, and when Teddy came running down the path, Rikki-tikki was ready to be petted.

paragraphs.context: very cunningly hidden, he found twenty-five eggs, about the size of a bantam’s eggs
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rikki-tikki finds Nagaina's eggs in the melon-bed. There are twenty-five of them.
paragraphs.simple: Rikki-tikki heard them going up the path from the stables, and he ran fast to the end of the melon-patch near the wall. There, in the warm litter around the melons, very cleverly hidden, he found twenty-five eggs. They were about the size of a bantam's eggs, but they had whitish skin instead of shell.

paragraphs.context: He had forgotten the egg. It still lay on the veranda
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nagaina takes the last egg and runs for her hole. Rikki-tikki follows her.
paragraphs.simple: He had forgotten the egg. It was still on the veranda, and Nagaina came nearer and nearer to it. At last, while Rikki-tikki was taking a breath, she took it in her mouth, turned to the veranda steps, and went down the path as fast as an arrow, with Rikki-tikki behind her. When a cobra runs for her life, she moves like a whip that is flicked across a horse's neck.

paragraphs.context: Kala Nag stood ten fair feet at the shoulders, and his tusks
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kala Nag is a very big elephant. His tusks are short, but he is strong in a fight.
paragraphs.simple: Kala Nag was a good ten feet high at the shoulders. His tusks had been cut off short, at five feet, and the ends had been wrapped with bands of copper so that they would not split. But he could do more with those short ends than any untrained elephant could do with real sharp tusks.

paragraphs.context: “Not green corn, Protector of the Poor —melons,” said Little Toomai
paragraphs.mainIdea: Little Toomai says that he took melons, not corn. The men laugh, and he wishes he could hide.
paragraphs.simple: “Not green corn, Protector of the Poor — melons,” said Little Toomai. All the men sitting around burst out in loud laughter. Most of them had taught their elephants that trick when they were boys. Little Toomai was hanging eight feet up in the air, and he wished very much that he were eight feet under the ground.

paragraphs.context: There was another roar of laughter, for that is an old joke among elephant-catchers
paragraphs.mainIdea: The hunters laugh because seeing elephants dance means never. No one has ever seen it.
paragraphs.simple: There was another roar of laughter, because that is an old joke among elephant-catchers, and it means just “never.” There are big flat cleared places hidden in the forests that are called elephants' ballrooms. But even these are found only by chance, and no man has ever seen the elephants dance. When a driver talks proudly about his skill and courage, the other drivers say, “And when did you see the elephants dance?”

paragraphs.context: At last Kala Nag stood still between two tree-trunks at the very top
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kala Nag takes Little Toomai to the top of a hill. There is an open space where the ground is hard from many feet.
paragraphs.simple: At last Kala Nag stood still between two tree-trunks at the very top. They were part of a circle of trees that grew around an open space of uneven shape, three or four acres big. In all of that space, as Little Toomai could see, the ground had been trampled as hard as a brick floor. Some trees stood in the middle of the open space, but their bark was rubbed off, and the white wood under it looked shiny and smooth in the patches of moonlight. Climbing plants hung from the high branches, and their flowers, big white waxy things like bells, hung down asleep. But in the open space there was not one blade of green, only trampled earth.

paragraphs.context: The morning broke in one sheet of pale yellow behind the green hills
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morning comes and the elephants go away. Only three elephants are left.
paragraphs.simple: Morning came as one sheet of pale yellow light behind the green hills, and the booming stopped at the first ray, as if the light had been an order. Before Little Toomai had got the ringing out of his head, and before he had even moved, there was no elephant in sight except Kala Nag, Pudmini, and the elephant with the rope-galls. There was no sign, no rustle and no whisper down the hillsides to show where the others had gone.

paragraphs.context: The camel doubled up camel-fashion, like a two-foot rule, and sat down whimpering
paragraphs.mainIdea: The camel sits down, and a big troop-horse arrives. He is angry about the camels.
paragraphs.simple: The camel folded up in the way camels do, like a two-foot ruler, and sat down, crying softly. In the dark there was a steady beat of hoofs, and a big troop-horse rode up at an easy run, as steadily as if he were on parade. He jumped over the tail of a gun and landed close to the mule.

paragraphs.context: They say that when a mule trips you can split a hen’s ear
paragraphs.mainIdea: Billy tells how mules work on mountains. They must keep hidden from the enemy.
paragraphs.simple: “They say that when a mule trips, you can split a hen's ear,” said Billy. “Now and then a badly packed saddle may make a mule fall, but that is very seldom. I wish I could show you our work. It is beautiful. It took me three years to find out what the men were trying to do. The skill of it is never to show yourself against the skyline, because if you do, someone may shoot at you. Remember that, young one. Always keep hidden as much as you can, even if you must go a mile out of your way. I lead the battery when it comes to that kind of climbing.”

paragraphs.context: That time or any other. Eating is always good
paragraphs.mainIdea: The gun-bullocks say that there is only one way to fight. They pull the big gun and eat grass.
paragraphs.simple: “At that time or any other time. Eating is always good. We eat until we are yoked up again, and then we pull the gun back to where Two Tails is waiting for it. Sometimes the big guns in the city fire back, and some of us are killed, and then there is more grass for those who are left. This is Fate, nothing but Fate. Still, Two Tails is a great coward. That is the right way to fight. We are brothers from Hapur. Our father was a sacred bull of Shiva. We have spoken.”

paragraphs.context: I never knew before what made Indian cattle so afraid of Englishmen
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer learns why Indian cattle fear Englishmen. They eat beef.
paragraphs.simple: Before this, I never knew why Indian cattle were so afraid of Englishmen. We eat beef, which no cattle-driver touches, and of course the cattle do not like that.

paragraphs.context: The rain began to fall again, and for a while it was too misty
paragraphs.mainIdea: The soldiers make a long line and move toward the Viceroy and the Amir. The ground shakes.
paragraphs.simple: The rain began to fall again, and for a while it was too misty what the soldiers were doing. They had made a big half-circle across the plain and were spreading out into a line. The line grew longer and longer until it was three-quarters of a mile from one end to the other, one solid wall of men, horses and guns. Then it came straight toward the Viceroy and the Amir, and as it got nearer, the ground began to shake, like the deck of a steamer when the engines are going fast.

paragraphs.context: Now Rann, the Kite, brings home the night
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the night song of the jungle. When night comes, the hunting animals are set free.
paragraphs.simple: Rann the kite brings the night home. Mang the bat lets the night go free. The farm animals are shut in their sheds and huts. The hunters are loose until morning. This is their proud hour. They have claws and teeth. They call good hunting to everyone who keeps the Jungle Law.

paragraphs.context: for Mowgli, the Frog, I will call thee
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mother Wolf decides to keep the human baby. She names him Mowgli the Frog and says he will one day hunt the tiger.
paragraphs.simple: Mother Wolf says to keep him. He came at night with no clothes, hungry and alone, and he was not afraid. He has already pushed one of her cubs aside. The lame tiger would have killed the baby and then run away, and the village would have hunted the wolves for revenge. She will keep him. She tells the baby to lie still, and she names him Mowgli the Frog. A time will come when he hunts Shere Khan, as Shere Khan hunted him.

paragraphs.context: As the dawn was breaking the Sambhur belled
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the hunting song of the wolf pack. At dawn they find a deer and chase it.
paragraphs.simple: At dawn a deer calls out. A female deer jumps up from a pond in the wood. A wolf who is scouting alone sees it and runs back to tell the waiting pack. The wolves find the deer and give the hunting cry on its track. They run without leaving a mark, and they can see in the dark. They call to one another to give the hunting cry again.

paragraphs.context: a lance, or a battering-ram, or a hammer
paragraphs.mainIdea: Kaa's whole body hits like a huge tool. The picture of a lance, a battering-ram, or a hammer is a picture of the python when he fights.
paragraphs.simple: Kaa comes straight in, fast and eager to kill. A python's blow comes from the head, with the weight of the whole body behind it. If you picture a lance, a battering-ram, or a hammer as heavy as half a ton, with a cool mind inside the handle, that is roughly what Kaa is like in a fight. Even a python a few feet long can knock a man down. Kaa is thirty feet long. His first blow goes into the crowd around Baloo, with his mouth shut, and he does not need a second blow. The monkeys scatter, crying his name and telling one another to run.

paragraphs.context: Here we go in a flung festoon
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the monkeys' road song. They boast as they swing in the trees, and the song laughs because they never do the great things they talk about.
paragraphs.simple: The monkeys swing up toward the moon in a hanging curve and wish they had extra hands and curly tails. They sit in a row and dream of noble deeds, but they only wish. They copy every sound they have heard from bat, beast, or bird, and they pretend they talk like men. Again and again the song says that a brother's tail hangs down behind. That is the way of the monkeys. They leap through the trees, make a grand noise, and say they are surely going to do splendid things.

paragraphs.context: Let the jungle listen to the things I have done
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the song Mowgli sings as he dances on Shere Khan's hide. He has killed the tiger, but both the village and the wolf pack have cast him out.
paragraphs.simple: Mowgli sings so the jungle will hear what he has done. Shere Khan said he would kill Mowgli the Frog at the gates in the dim evening. Mowgli tells him to drink deep, because he will not drink again, and to sleep and dream of the kill. Mowgli is alone on the grazing ground. He calls Gray Brother and the Lone Wolf, because there is big game. He tells them to bring the buffalo bulls and to drive them as he orders. He asks if Shere Khan is still asleep, and he comes with the bulls behind him. Rama the buffalo stamps. Mowgli asks the river where Shere Khan went. He cannot dig like a porcupine, fly like a peacock, or hang like a bat. The bamboos tell him. The lame tiger lies under Rama's feet. Mowgli tells him to get up and kill, then says he is asleep and they will not wake him. The kites come down and the black ants come up. Mowgli has no cloth. He is ashamed to be naked before all these, so he asks to borrow the striped coat for the Council Rock. He made a promise, and only the coat is still needed. With a hunter's knife he bends down for his gift. He asks the river to see that Shere Khan gives the coat. He tells Gray Brother and Akela to pull, because the hide is heavy. The village people are angry. They throw stones and talk like children. His mouth bleeds. He tells his brothers to run with him through the hot night, away from the village lights, toward the low moon. The village has cast him out, though he did them no harm. They were afraid. The wolf pack has cast him out too. The jungle is shut and the village gates are shut. He goes between the village and the jungle as a bat goes between beasts and birds. He dances on the hide. His heart is heavy. His mouth is cut by the stones, but his heart is light because he is back in the jungle. The two feelings fight in him like snakes in the spring. Water comes from his eyes, yet he laughs. He is two Mowglis, and the hide is under his feet. All the jungle knows he has killed Shere Khan. He tells the wolves to look. His heart is heavy with things he does not understand.

paragraphs.context: hush thee, my baby, the night is behind us
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is a mother seal's lullaby. She tells her baby that the storm and the shark will not wake him.
paragraphs.simple: A mother tells her baby to be quiet. The night is behind them, and the water that was green is now black. The moon looks down over the waves to find them resting in the hollows. Where wave meets wave, that is his soft pillow. She tells the little one to curl up and rest. The storm will not wake him, and a shark will not catch him. He can sleep in the arms of the slow, swinging sea.

paragraphs.context: your head will be sunk by your heels
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is a short song for a baby seal. He must not swim yet, because the sea is dangerous for him.
paragraphs.simple: The baby must not swim until he is six weeks old, or his head will sink and his heels will go up. Summer gales and killer whales are bad for baby seals. He should splash and grow strong. Then he cannot be wrong. He is a child of the open sea.

paragraphs.context: the great deep-sea song that all the St
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is Lukannon, the sad song the seals sing on the way back to their beaches. It remembers the time before the hunters came.
paragraphs.simple: The book says this is the sad deep-sea song the seals sing when they head back to their beaches in summer. An old seal meets his friends in the morning where the summer waves roar on the rock shelves. He hears them lift the song. Two million voices sing of the beaches of Lukannon. They sing of pleasant places by the salt lakes, of groups shuffling down the sand hills, and of midnight dances that stirred the sea until it looked like flame. That was before the seal hunters came. He will never meet those friends again. They came and went in huge crowds that darkened the shore. As far as a voice could reach, they called to the ones who were landing and sang them up the beach. Tall winter wheat grew there, wet plants hung, and sea fog soaked everything. The flat rocks of their playground were smooth and worn. It was the home where they were born. Now he meets only a broken, scattered band. Men shoot them in the water and club them on the land. Men drive them to the Salt House like tame sheep. Still they sing the old song, from before the hunters came. He tells Gooverooska to wheel south and tell the deep-sea leaders their sad story. Soon the beaches will be as empty as a shark's egg thrown on shore, and they will not know their sons any more.

paragraphs.context: Proud of my lilt through the sky
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is Darzee's song of thanks. The tailor-bird praises Rikki-tikki because the cobra danger is dead.
paragraphs.simple: Darzee says he is a singer and a tailor. He is proud of his song in the sky and of the nest he sews. He tells the mother to sing to her babies again and to lift her head. The evil that troubled them is dead, and the terror that hid in the roses has been thrown on the rubbish heap. He asks who saved them, and he asks for that one's nest and name. It is brave, true Rikki-tikki, the hunter. Darzee gives him the thanks of the birds, bowing with his tail feathers spread. He will not leave the praise to a nightingale. He himself will sing the praise of Rikki with the red eyes.

paragraphs.context: Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the song Toomai's mother sings to her baby. Shiv gives every creature its share, even the little grasshopper Parbati tried to hide.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago Shiv poured out the harvest and made the winds blow. He gave each one a share of food, work, and fate, from the king on his seat to the beggar at the gate. He made everything. He made a thorn for the camel, fodder for the cattle, and a mother's love for a sleepy child. He gave wheat to rich people and millet to the poor, broken scraps to holy men who beg from door to door, cattle to the tiger, dead meat to the kite, and rags and bones to the wolves outside the wall at night. Nothing was too high and no one was too low. Parbati watched beside him. She thought she would trick him. She stole a little grasshopper and hid it in her breast. When the giving was over, she asked, laughing, whether one mouth of a million was still unfed. Shiv laughed and said everyone had a share, even the little one hidden by her heart. She took it out and saw that the smallest thing had eaten a new leaf. She was afraid and prayed to Shiv, who has given food to all that live. The song says again that he made all things, and a mother's heart for her little son.

paragraphs.context: We lent to Alexander the strength of Hercules
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the parade song of the camp animals. Elephants, bullocks, horses, mules, and camels each sing about the work they do for the army.
paragraphs.simple: The elephants of the gun team say they lent their strength, the wisdom of their foreheads, and the cunning of their knees, and their necks were never set free again. They ask for way for the big gun teams. The gun bullocks say the other animals fear a cannonball and are upset by gunpowder, but they themselves pull the guns. They ask for way for the twenty pairs of the gun team. The cavalry horses say the finest tune, played by the horse soldiers, is sweeter to them than the calls for stables or water. They want to be fed, trained, handled, and groomed, and to have good riders and room, and to go out in lines to the war song. The mules say they scrambled up a hill when the path was lost in rolling stones, and they still went on. They can twist and climb and turn up anywhere, and a spare leg is their delight on a mountain. Good luck to the sergeant who lets them pick the road, and bad luck to drivers who cannot tie a load. The food-carrying camels say they have no tune of their own. Every neck is like a hairy horn, and their marching song is Can't, Don't, Shan't, Won't. Someone's pack has slid off, someone's load has tipped in the road, and there is a noisy halt. Then all the beasts sing together. They are children of the camp, each serving in his own place, children of the yoke, the goad, the pack, and the load. Their line across the flat land is like a heel rope bent again. It reaches and rolls far, sweeping everything away to war. The dusty, silent men who walk beside them cannot tell why they march and suffer day by day.

sentences.context: Even the tiger hides when little Tabaqui goes mad
sentences.simple: When Tabaqui goes mad, even the tiger hides.
sentences.grammar: 'Even' stresses a surprise: the tiger is the strongest animal, but he hides. 'When' starts a clause about time.

sentences.context: The fool has had no more sense than to jump at a woodcutters’ campfire
sentences.simple: The fool had so little sense that he jumped at a woodcutters' campfire.
sentences.grammar: 'No more sense than to jump...' means 'only enough sense to jump', and says the tiger acted in a silly way.

sentences.context: A wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg
sentences.simple: A wolf who is used to carrying his own cubs can hold an egg in his mouth, if he has to.
sentences.grammar: 'Accustomed to moving' is a short form of 'who is accustomed to moving'; 'if necessary' is a short form of 'if it is necessary'.

sentences.context: was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub
sentences.simple: Has any wolf ever been able to say proudly that she has a man's cub among her children?
sentences.grammar: This is a question that expects the answer 'no'. 'Was there ever...?' means 'there never was...'.

sentences.context: Shere Khan might have faced Father Wolf, but he could not stand up
sentences.simple: Shere Khan could perhaps have fought Father Wolf, but he could not fight Mother Wolf.
sentences.grammar: 'Might have + past participle' (might have faced) talks about something that was possible in the past, but did not happen.

sentences.context: it is the man-cub who has lived too long
sentences.simple: It is the man-cub who has lived too long.
sentences.grammar: This is a cleft sentence: 'It is ... who ...' puts stress on the man-cub as the one who should not have lived this long.

sentences.context: Shere Khan would flatter them and wonder that such fine young hunters
sentences.simple: Shere Khan used to say nice things to them that were not true, and he would say it was strange that such fine young hunters were happy to be led by a dying wolf and a man's cub.
sentences.grammar: 'Would + verb' tells what happened again and again in the past. 'Wonder that...' is followed by a that-clause.

sentences.context: all but your brother in blood, I promise that when I am a man
sentences.simple: I was almost your brother by blood, so I promise that when I am a man among men, I will not betray you.
sentences.grammar: 'All but' means 'almost'. After 'when' we use the present tense (I am) for the future, as in 'when I am a man'.

sentences.context: The big, serious, old brown bear was delighted to have so quick a pupil
sentences.simple: The big, serious, old brown bear was very happy to have a pupil who learned so fast.
sentences.grammar: 'So quick a pupil' puts 'a' after the adjective: 'so + adjective + a + noun'. It means 'a pupil who is so quick'.

sentences.context: Better he should be bruised from head to foot by me who love him
sentences.simple: It is better that he is hurt all over by me, who love him, than that he comes to harm through ignorance.
sentences.grammar: 'Better he should be...than that he should...' is a short form of 'It is better that he should be... than that he should...'.

sentences.context: Had they been alone they could have gone twice as fast
sentences.simple: If they had been alone, they could have gone twice as fast.
sentences.grammar: 'Had they been...' means 'If they had been...'. It talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Unless and until they drop him from the branches in sport
sentences.simple: As long as they do not drop him from the branches for fun, or kill him because they have nothing to do, I have no fear for the man-cub.
sentences.grammar: 'Unless and until' means 'if they do not... and up to the time when they do'. The main clause 'I have no fear' comes after it.

sentences.context: I am more likely to give help than to ask it
sentences.simple: I will help more often than I ask for help.
sentences.grammar: 'More ... than ...' compares two things: 'to give help' is compared with 'to ask it'. 'Likely to + verb' says that something will probably happen.

sentences.context: Would that Baloo were here; but we must do what we can
sentences.simple: I wish that Baloo were here; but we must do what we can.
sentences.grammar: 'Would that + past' (were) is an old way to say 'I wish that...'. It talks about something that is not true now.

sentences.context: Kaa was everything that the monkeys feared in the jungle
sentences.simple: Kaa was all the things that the monkeys were afraid of in the jungle.
sentences.grammar: 'Everything that the monkeys feared' has a relative clause ('that the monkeys feared') that tells which things.

sentences.context: In a little time, had I stayed, I should have walked down his throat
sentences.simple: In a short time, if I had stayed, I would have walked down his throat.
sentences.grammar: 'Had I stayed' means 'If I had stayed'. 'Should have walked' (here the same as 'would have') says what would have happened, but did not.

sentences.context: Mowgli had not the faintest idea of the difference that caste makes
sentences.simple: Mowgli did not have the smallest idea of the difference that caste makes between one man and another.
sentences.grammar: 'Had not' is an old way to make a negative: it means 'did not have'. The relative clause 'that caste makes' tells which difference.

sentences.context: If thou art so wise, better bring his hide to Khanhiwara
sentences.simple: If you are so wise, you had better bring his hide to Khanhiwara.
sentences.grammar: 'If thou art' is an old way of saying 'if you are'. 'Better bring' is a short form of 'You had better bring', which gives advice.

sentences.context: I might have known that thou wouldst not forget me
sentences.simple: I should have known that you would not forget me.
sentences.grammar: 'Might have + past participle' here means 'could have known'. It says that Mowgli did not think about it, but should have.

sentences.context: slipped off Rama’s neck, laying about him right and left
sentences.simple: Mowgli waited for the right time, then slid off Rama's neck and hit out on both sides with his stick.
sentences.grammar: 'Laying about him right and left' uses a present participle to say what he did at the same time as he slipped off.

sentences.context: if he had been ten years younger he would have taken his chance
sentences.simple: To be fair to Buldeo, if he had been ten years younger, he would have faced Akela.
sentences.grammar: This is a third conditional: 'if + had been..., would have + past participle'. It talks about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Not for nothing are ye called the Free People
sentences.simple: You are called the Free People for a good reason.
sentences.grammar: 'Not for nothing' puts the negative first, so the verb comes before the subject: 'are ye called'. It means 'for a good reason'.

sentences.context: Sea Catch had just finished his forty-fifth fight one spring when Matkah
sentences.simple: One spring, Sea Catch had just finished his forty-fifth fight when Matkah came up out of the sea.
sentences.grammar: 'Had just finished' is the past perfect: it shows that one action was finished before another action (Matkah came) in the past.

sentences.context: Little seals can no more swim than little children
sentences.simple: Little seals cannot swim, just as little children cannot swim.
sentences.grammar: 'No more ... than ...' means 'also not'. It says that two things are both not true.

sentences.context: if you seals will come here year after year, of course the men
sentences.simple: If you seals come here every year, the men will of course learn about it.
sentences.grammar: Here 'if you will come' means 'if you keep coming'. 'Get to know' means 'begin to know'.

sentences.context: the only seal, black or white, who ever thought of looking for new islands
sentences.simple: the only seal, black or white, who ever thought of looking for new islands.
sentences.grammar: The relative clause 'who ever thought of...' tells which seal. 'Thought of + -ing' (looking) is a verb with 'of' and a verb in the -ing form.

sentences.context: Kotick had never fasted for four months as the big seals did every year
sentences.simple: Kotick had never gone without food for four months, as the big seals did each year.
sentences.grammar: 'Had never fasted' is the past perfect with 'never': it says that this had not happened before that time. 'As' compares with the big seals.

sentences.context: I’ve done my best for you these five seasons past
sentences.simple: I have done my best for you for the last five seasons.
sentences.grammar: 'These five seasons past' shows a time up to now. The present perfect 'I've done' goes with it.

sentences.context: Rikki-tikki knew better than to waste time in staring
sentences.simple: Rikki-tikki was wise enough not to waste time looking.
sentences.grammar: 'Knew better than to + verb' means 'was wise enough not to do it'.

sentences.context: If Teddy doesn’t pick him up by the tail, or try to put him
sentences.simple: If Teddy does not pick him up by the tail or try to put him in a cage, he will run in and out of the house all day.
sentences.grammar: This is a first conditional: 'if + present (doesn't pick up), will + verb (he'll run)'. It talks about what is likely.

sentences.context: If I could get up to your nest, I’d roll all your babies out
sentences.simple: If I could get up to your nest, I would roll all your babies out.
sentences.grammar: This is a second conditional: 'if + past (could), would + verb'. It talks about something that is not likely.

sentences.context: Not eat exactly; no. Darzee, if you have a grain of sense
sentences.simple: No, I do not exactly eat them.
sentences.grammar: This answer leaves out the subject and the helper verb: 'Not eat exactly' means 'I will not exactly eat them'.

sentences.context: Rikki-tikki had a right to be proud of himself
sentences.simple: Rikki-tikki had good reason to be proud of himself.
sentences.grammar: 'Had a right to + verb' means 'had a good reason to do it'.

sentences.context: he knew that the minute they were hatched they could each kill a man
sentences.simple: He knew that, as soon as they came out of the eggs, each of them could kill a man or a mongoose.
sentences.grammar: 'The minute + clause' works like 'as soon as'. 'Were hatched' is the passive form.

sentences.context: Kala Nag would no more have dreamed of disobeying his shrill little orders
sentences.simple: Kala Nag would never have thought of not obeying his sharp, high little orders.
sentences.grammar: 'Would no more have dreamed of ... than ...' means 'would never have thought of'. It compares with the other thing that is not true.

sentences.context: that thou must needs go elephant-catching on thy own account
sentences.simple: Are good brick elephant-lines and a little tent-carrying not enough for you? Must you go catching elephants too?
sentences.grammar: This is a question with 'not' put in front of the subject ('Are not ... enough'). 'Must needs' is an old way of saying 'must'. 'Thou' means 'you'.

sentences.context: Anyone but a mudhead who never saw the jungle would know
sentences.simple: Everyone except a fool who has never seen the jungle would know that.
sentences.grammar: 'Anyone but a mudhead' means 'everyone except a fool'. The relative clause 'who never saw the jungle' tells more about the mudhead.

sentences.context: a private soldier would feel if he had been called out of the ranks
sentences.simple: He felt as an ordinary soldier would feel if his chief had called him out of the line and praised him.
sentences.grammar: 'As ... would feel if he had been called' compares his feeling to an imagined case. 'If he had been called' is the passive past perfect.

sentences.context: so far away that it sounded no more than a pinhole of noise
sentences.simple: It was so far away that it sounded like only a very small hole of sound in the quiet.
sentences.grammar: 'So far away that ...' shows result: 'so + adjective/adverb + that + clause'. 'No more than' means 'only'.

sentences.context: What never man has seen he has seen through the long night
sentences.simple: He has seen, through the long night, what no man has ever seen.
sentences.grammar: The object 'What never man has seen' is put first, and 'never' comes before 'man'. This is not usual order; it adds force.

sentences.context: Imagine the feelings of Sunol if a car-horse called her a “skate,”
sentences.simple: Think how Sunol would feel if a horse that pulls a street car called her a 'skate'.
sentences.grammar: 'Imagine' starts a command, and 'if + past (called)' makes an imagined case. The writer asks the reader to compare the two feelings.

sentences.context: Before I’d lie down, not to speak of sitting down
sentences.simple: I would never lie down, and much less sit down, and let a man fire over me.
sentences.grammar: 'Before I'd + verb' means 'I would never...'. 'Not to speak of' adds a stronger case: if lying down is bad, sitting is worse.

sentences.context: if I was like him I could pull the guns
sentences.simple: If I were like my captain, I could pull the guns.
sentences.grammar: 'If I was like him' is a second conditional that talks about something that is not true. Many speakers use 'was' for 'were'.

sentences.context: I know just enough to be uncomfortable, and not enough to go on
sentences.simple: I know only enough to feel bad, and not enough to go on in spite of it.
sentences.grammar: 'Enough to + verb' tells how much is needed. The two parts are joined by 'and not' to show a difference.

sentences.context: Unless you have been there you cannot imagine what a frightening effect
sentences.simple: If you have not been there, you cannot imagine how frightening this is.
sentences.grammar: 'Unless' means 'if not'. 'What a ... effect' is an exclamation inside the clause that follows 'imagine'.

sentences.context: Would it were so in Afghanistan
sentences.simple: I wish it were like this in Afghanistan.
sentences.grammar: 'Would it were...' is an old way to say 'I wish it were...'. It talks about something that is not true.

all but.example: He is our brother in all but blood

back out.example: he backed out of the cave-mouth growling

carry off.example: the tiger carried off a man at twilight

cast out.example: I have been cast out of the Pack

come across.example: he had come across more than one such barricade

come back.example: Not one small wolfling has come back to thank old Baloo

drive out.meaning: To make someone leave a place.

fly at.example: very ready to fly at an intruder

for fear of.example: for fear of those that love thee

for the sake of.example: for the sake of the bull that bought thee

get away.example: the other seal might get away if he could

get rid of.meaning: To make something go away, or to stop having it.
get rid of.example: to get rid of the sleepy feeling in the tips

give tongue.example: Akela gave tongue in the full hunting-yell

go back.example: thou must go back to men at last

go off.meaning: To fire, as a gun does, with a loud sound.
go off.example: The old Tower musket went off with a bang

good hunting.meaning: A jungle greeting. It wishes someone a good hunt.
good hunting.example: Good hunting all That keep the Jungle Law

had better.meaning: Used to say what is the wise thing to do.
had better.example: Mowgli had better be set to work as soon as possible

hand over.meaning: To give something to someone else.
hand over.example: had not been handed over to him

head off.meaning: To get in front of animals and turn them another way.
head off.example: Head off that drove of four-year-olds

head over heels.example: knocking the youngsters head over heels right and left

hold on.example: he held on as the body cartwhipped over the floor

in a hurry.example: he was in a hurry to go back to Novastoshnah

in spite of.meaning: Even though something makes it hard.
in spite of.example: not enough to go on in spite of it

in the least.meaning: At all. It is used with a negative word.
in the least.example: which he did not in the least understand

keep one's temper.meaning: To stay calm and not get angry.

lay out.example: to lay out Shere Khan’s hide upon the Council Rock

look out for.meaning: To be careful and watch for danger.

look to it.meaning: To make sure that something is done.
look to it.example: look to it then that thou dost not kill the man-cub

look up.meaning: To lift your eyes to see something above you.
look up.example: Baloo looked up to see where the voice came from

look well.meaning: The wolves' call at the council. It means look carefully.

lose one's temper.example: Kotick began to lose his temper

make fun of.meaning: To laugh at someone in an unkind way.
make fun of.example: made fun of the drivers who were going away

make sure.meaning: To check that something is true or safe.
make sure.example: gave the Call a second time to make sure

make up.meaning: To invent something, such as a song.
make up.example: Mowgli made up a song without any rhymes

man's cub.meaning: A human child. The animals call Mowgli this.
man's cub.example: accept the man's cub according to the Law

no more than.example: I saw no more than a big snake

on account of.example: on account of the new elephants

on the trail of.meaning: Following the marks that someone or something leaves.
on the trail of.example: on the trail of the Bandar-log

out of reach.meaning: Too far for you to touch it.

pick and choose.meaning: To choose only the things that you like best.

pick up.meaning: To lift something from the place where it is.
pick up.example: pick up a wicker pot plastered inside with earth

put on.example: I put on my boots and waterproof

red flower.meaning: The animals' name for fire. They are afraid to say fire.
red flower.example: By Red Flower Bagheera meant fire

right and left.example: Bagheera killed right and left as he felt hungry

run away.meaning: To leave a place fast, because of fear.
run away.example: run away as soon as they can repeat the Hunting Verse

set off.example: before he set off on his last exploration

set out.meaning: To start to do something, or to start a journey.
set out.example: They set out together across the Pacific

show off.meaning: To do something so that people will look at you and think well of you.

take care.example: taking care to crush the young cobras

take orders.meaning: To do what someone tells you to do.

tired of.meaning: No longer wanting to do something, because you have done it too much.

to and fro.meaning: One way and then the other way, again and again.
to and fro.example: Drive them to and fro as I order

turn into.example: Mowgli turn into a tiger, too

turn out.meaning: To make someone leave a place.
turn out.example: Mowgli was turned out of the Seeonee wolf-pack

wind up.example: Baloo wound up, patting his big furry stomach

work one's way.meaning: To move on slowly, with great effort.
work one's way.example: worked his way desperately, inch by inch

might as well.meaning: There is no strong reason not to.
might as well.example: I may as well give you something on account now

set to work.example: Mowgli had better be set to work

a good deal.example: had to learn a great deal more

make up one's mind.example: trying to make up his mind to run

at hand.meaning: Near. Close enough to reach now.
at hand.example: Baloo must be at hand; Bagheera would not have come

may as well.meaning: There is no strong reason not to. You could do it.
may as well.example: morning; but I may as well give you something on
